title: Government Closely Monitoring Seasonal Influenza Trends Across the Country
subtitle:
No Cause for Panic: Seasonal Influenza Remains Self-Limiting; No New or Unusual Virus Strain Detected, Says DG ICMR Dr. Rajiv Bahl
H1N1 in India Shows Expected Seasonal Changes, No Unusual Genetic Shift Detected
body_text:
The Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW), in coordination with the Department of Health Research (DHR), Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) and National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC), is closely monitoring the prevailing seasonal respiratory illness trends across the country through a robust pan-India surveillance network.
Addressing the media in New Delhi, Secretary, Department of Health Research (DHR) and Director General, ICMR, Dr. Rajiv Bahl stated that the current influenza situation is being continuously monitored and that there is no cause for panic or alarm. The influenza viruses currently circulating in the country are consistent with the seasonal pattern observed in recent years.
The ongoing genomic and epidemiological surveillance through the network of 73 DHR-ICMR Virus Research and Diagnostic Laboratories (VRDLs) has provided important reassurance.
The circulating Influenza A (H1N1) viruses have been identified as A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1) pdm09-like viruses . Hemagglutinin (HA) gene analysis places the isolates in clade 6B.1A.5a2a; subclade D.3.1.1 .
Dr. Bahl informed that this lineage has been in continuous circulation in India since 2025 . The genetic changes observed are consistent with the normal antigenic drift seen in seasonal influenza viruses. Such minor genetic changes occur routinely as influenza viruses circulate and, by themselves, do not indicate the emergence of a new or dangerous strain.
Dr. Bahl emphasised that the present observations therefore do not indicate the emergence of a new influenza threat and are consistent with the expected behaviour of seasonal influenza viruses.
Seasonal influenza, including Influenza A (H1N1), is predominantly a mild and self-limiting respiratory illness in otherwise healthy individuals. Common symptoms include: Fever, Cough, Sore throat, Headache, Body ache, Fatigue and weakness.
In most people, symptoms improve with supportive care and adequate rest and hydration. The presence of H1N1 does not, by itself, mean that a person will develop severe disease or require hospitalisation. Dr. Bahl said that while seasonal influenza is generally mild, certain individuals have a higher risk of developing complications. These include: Elderly persons, young children, individuals with underlying medical conditions or co-morbidities and persons with compromised immunity. He advised such individuals to exercise greater caution and seek timely medical advice if they develop influenza-like symptoms.
He also advised the public at large to follow routine respiratory hygiene and infection-prevention measures:
DOs:
Cover the mouth and nose while coughing or sneezing. Wash hands frequently with soap and water or use an appropriate hand sanitiser. Stay at home when unwell and avoid close contact with others. Maintain adequate hydration and take sufficient rest. Consume a healthy and balanced diet. Seek medical advice if symptoms are severe, persistent or worsening. Follow medical advice regarding testing or treatment.
Don’ts:
Do not panic because of the detection of H1N1. Do not take antivirals or antibiotics without medical advice. Avoid close contact with others while symptomatic. Avoid touching the eyes, nose and mouth with unwashed hands.
The Union Health Ministry, DHR, ICMR and NCDC are maintaining continuous epidemiological, virological and genomic surveillance to monitor influenza trends across the country. The extensive VRDL network enables timely detection and characterisation of circulating respiratory viruses and helps public health authorities respond appropriately to any emerging trends.
The surveillance mechanism will continue to closely track changes in influenza activity, circulating strains and disease severity.
The current evidence, however, does not indicate any unusual change in the behaviour of H1N1 influenza or the emergence of a new strain.
The public is therefore advised to remain informed and vigilant, but not alarmed . Seasonal influenza is a familiar and routinely monitored respiratory infection, and adherence to simple preventive measures, timely medical consultation when required, and avoidance of unnecessary medication can help protect individuals and communities.
*****
SR
HFW/ Update on Influenza A (H1N1) virus surveillance /25 August 2026/3

ministry.name: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare

enrichment.summary: The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, along with ICMR-DHR and NCDC, briefed the media that seasonal influenza, including circulating H1N1 strains, is being closely monitored across India and follows the expected seasonal pattern with no unusual strain emergence. DG ICMR Dr. Rajiv Bahl said genomic surveillance via 73 DHR-ICMR Virus Research and Diagnostic Laboratories (VRDLs) identified circulating H1N1 as A/Missouri/11/2025-like viruses (clade 6B.1A.5a2a, subclade D.3.1.1), showing normal antigenic drift rather than a new dangerous strain. The public was advised to remain vigilant but not alarmed, follow basic hygiene practices, and seek medical advice for severe or persistent symptoms.
enrichment.context:
India has a structured pan-India surveillance architecture for respiratory and emerging infectious diseases, built around the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP) under NCDC and the network of Virus Research and Diagnostic Laboratories (VRDLs) supported by ICMR-DHR. This system, strengthened significantly after the 2009 H1N1 pandemic and further expanded post-COVID-19, enables real-time genomic and epidemiological tracking of circulating viruses, allowing health authorities to distinguish routine seasonal variation (antigenic drift) from the emergence of genuinely novel or more virulent strains (antigenic shift). Such distinctions are critical for public health messaging, as false alarms can cause unnecessary panic, hospital overcrowding, and misuse of antivirals, while under-detection of genuine threats could delay response.

This release is essentially a reassurance communication rather than an announcement of new policy or a major scientific finding, but it does illustrate India's institutional capacity for genomic surveillance of influenza, referencing WHO-style nomenclature (clade/subclade classification) and the role of ICMR-DHR-NCDC coordination. It also reinforces WHO's Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System (GISRS) framework, which India participates in for strain characterization and vaccine strain selection guidance.

prelims_questions.question: The Virus Research and Diagnostic Laboratories (VRDL) network mentioned in context of influenza surveillance in India is coordinated by which organisation?
prelims_questions.explanation: The release states the VRDL network of 73 laboratories operates under the Department of Health Research (DHR)-ICMR, providing genomic and epidemiological surveillance of circulating viruses.

prelims_questions.question: 'Antigenic drift' in the context of influenza viruses refers to:
options: Emergence of an entirely new subtype through genetic reassortment
Minor, gradual genetic changes occurring routinely as the virus circulates
Complete disappearance of a viral strain from circulation
Transmission of the virus from animals to humans for the first time
prelims_questions.explanation: The release explains that the genetic changes observed in circulating H1N1 are consistent with normal antigenic drift, i.e., routine minor genetic changes, not the emergence of a new strain.

mains_questions.question: Discuss the institutional framework for disease surveillance in India, highlighting the role of ICMR, NCDC, and the VRDL network in early detection and response to seasonal and emerging infectious diseases.

Examine the importance of genomic surveillance in distinguishing routine seasonal variations in viruses from the emergence of novel pathogenic strains, with reference to India's preparedness for future outbreaks.

study_notes.reason: The release carries a concrete testable factual core (VRDL network, ICMR-DHR-NCDC structure, clade/subclade nomenclature) while also illustrating India's surveillance architecture and the antigenic drift vs shift distinction, which supports analytical health-governance questions.

prelims.point: 73 DHR-ICMR Virus Research and Diagnostic Laboratories (VRDLs) form the genomic/epidemiological surveillance network for influenza in India
prelims.why_important: VRDL network size and role under ICMR-DHR is a concrete institutional fact UPSC could test in a statement-based question.

prelims.point: Circulating H1N1 strain identified as A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1)pdm09-like virus, clade 6B.1A.5a2a, subclade D.3.1.1
prelims.why_important: Illustrates WHO-style clade/subclade nomenclature used in influenza characterization, a concept UPSC could probe via a distinction-type question.

prelims.point: NCDC (National Centre for Disease Control) and ICMR-DHR jointly coordinate with MoHFW on disease surveillance
prelims.why_important: Institutional mandate and coordination structure among health bodies is a recurring prelims theme (which body does what).

prelims.point: Distinction between antigenic drift (minor, routine mutation) and antigenic shift (major genetic change producing a novel strain)
prelims.why_important: This is a classic confusable-concept pair examiners favour for objective questions on virology/epidemiology.

mains.point: Robust genomic surveillance infrastructure (VRDL-IDSP network) enables India to distinguish routine seasonal variation from emerging pandemic threats, strengthening early-warning capacity built post-2009 H1N1 and post-COVID
mains.theme: Public health surveillance and pandemic preparedness
mains.analytical_use: Useful for a question on India's institutional preparedness for infectious disease outbreaks or lessons learnt from past pandemics.

mains.point: Balancing risk communication: avoiding both public panic/misuse of antivirals from over-alarm and under-detection risks from complacency
mains.analytical_use: Could support a question on challenges in public health messaging during disease outbreaks.

mains.point: India's participation in WHO's Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System (GISRS) links domestic surveillance to global strain characterization and vaccine strain selection
mains.analytical_use: Relevant for questions on India's role in global health governance frameworks.
